short: Fifty years in which the empire nearly came apart: some twenty-six emperors, plague, invasion, and a currency that stopped meaning anything.
full:
Between 235 and 284 the empire had around twenty-six men the Senate recognised as emperor, and many more who claimed it. Almost all died violently. The army made and unmade them faster than any of them could govern, and each new claimant had to buy the loyalty of the troops who had just killed his predecessor.

Everything failed at once. The Sasanian Persians captured the emperor Valerian alive in 260 — an humiliation without precedent. Germanic groups crossed the Rhine and Danube more or less at will. The Plague of Cyprian killed on a scale nobody could count. To pay the soldiers, emperors debased the silver coinage until the denarius held almost no silver at all, and the price of everything ran away from the people paying it.

The empire also physically split: a Gallic Empire in the west and Palmyra in the east both broke away and ruled themselves for years. That it was reassembled at all is the surprising part. Aurelian took back the lost provinces in the 270s, and Diocletian rebuilt the state on entirely different foundations after 284.
